chunks: "I compare them on accuracy, loss, bandwidth, DC capability, isolation and cost.
A shunt resistor with a current sense amp is the default: very accurate, linear, DC to hundreds of kilohertz, cheap, and small.
Its costs are I to the 2R loss, a voltage drop in the path, and no isolation. It scales badly above about 50 to 100 amps.
Sensing across a MOSFET's Rds(on) or an inductor's DCR is free in terms of loss and parts, but it's only accurate to maybe 10 to 20 percent because the resistance moves with temperature.
That's fine for overcurrent protection and peak current mode, not for metering.
Magnetic sensors, Hall and current transformers, give isolation and negligible loss and can handle hundreds of amps.
But they cost more, take more board space, have offset and temperature drift, and are poor at small currents. A CT is AC only.
So my rule: low voltage and moderate current, shunt plus CSA. Need isolation or very high current, Hall or CT. Just need a trip point, use Rds(on) or the inductor.
The deciding factors are always accuracy at the smallest current I care about, power budget, and whether there's a safety barrier."
